abstract: The expression of many biological traits depends on environmental conditions, physiological state, or age. Such traits are naturally described as function-valued traits. Conditions determining whether their gradual evolution leads to a single stable phenotype or to phenotypic diversification have been suitably established for finite-dimensional traits. Yet, function-valued traits can also be infinite-dimensional, as with continuous age-structure, and their analysis remains challenging. Here, we extend invasion analysis to infinite-dimensional function-valued traits. We derive conditions for identifying candidate evolutionary endpoints, determining whether selection draws nearby populations toward them (convergence stability), and assessing whether, once reached, these endpoints resist invasion by nearby mutants (local uninvadability) or may instead allow evolutionary branching. These conditions depend on the selection gradient, the Jacobian of the selection gradient, and the Hessian of invasion fitness. For finite-dimensional traits, a negative-definite Jacobian of the selection gradient guarantees convergence stability regardless of genetic covariances, while a negative-definite Hessian of invasion fitness guarantees uninvadability. In infinite dimensions, we show that these sufficient conditions require strong rather than ordinary negative definiteness. We then focus on the particular case of life-history traits, for which investment at one age can alter physiological states and thereby affect fitness at later ages. Using optimal-control theory, we derive expressions for the Jacobian and Hessian operators that account for these indirect effects. We illustrate our theoretical results with two models of floral investment, with and without state dynamics. Individual-based simulations complement these analyses, showing that evolutionary branching can indeed occur when the theory identifies it as a possibility.
